Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Elderly people with prediabetes receiving weekly vitamin D3 had lower depression scores (PHQ-9) than controls at 6 months.
Sentence: "Supplemented participants demonstrated lower mean PHQ-9 scores compared to controls at 6 (15.69 ± 6.15 vs. 19.77 ± 8.96, p = 0.021) and 12 months (13.52 ± 5.01 vs. 20.20 ± 8.67, p < 0.001)."
Measured as: PHQ-9 score at 6 months
Population: Elderly people with prediabetes (mean age ~73-74 years)
Intervention: Vitamin D3 25,000 IU weekly for 12 months, plus lifestyle measures
Comparator: No supplementation, plus lifestyle measures
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 90
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: harm
Claim: In PD patients given vitamin D3, folic acid and B12 for 6 months, the 15D depression dimension score significantly increased (improved) from baseline.
Sentence: "After the intervention, the mean score of speech, mental function, discomfort and symptoms, depression, and QoL significantly increased (p < 0.05 for all)."
Measured as: depression (15D dimension score)
Population: Levodopa-treated Parkinson's disease patients in Romania, mean age 71 years
Intervention: Daily tablet with 800 IU vitamin D3, 1000 µg folic acid, 15 µg vitamin B12 for 6 months
Comparator: None (single-arm, baseline vs 6 months)
Design: case series
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

  "rationale": "Both studies actually found an improvement in depression, and the conflict is apparent because Study B measured the single depression item of the 15D quality-of-life instrument (where higher scores mean better health, misclassified as harm under a 'lower is better' outcome) rather than a full depression scale like Study A's PHQ-9.",
